/**
 * @generated by patterns — regenerate rather than edit.
 * @pattern specification
 * @options e284827a0b48e403
 */

/**
 * What the rules are about.
 *
 * A concrete type rather than a type parameter, because a specification is only
 * worth naming when it is a rule about something in particular. The `status`
 * field is a literal union on purpose: it is what lets a rule refine, since
 * narrowing to `"paid"` says something a `string` could not.
 */
export interface Order {
  readonly id: string;
  readonly total: number;
  readonly status: "draft" | "paid" | "cancelled";
}

/**
 * One comparison, as data.
 *
 * The reason the leaves are declarative rather than arbitrary functions: a
 * closure can be run but not read, so a rule expressed as one cannot be handed
 * to anything that does not already agree to call it. This can be read, and
 * that is the whole of what translation needs.
 */
export interface OrderCriterion {
  readonly field: keyof Order;
  readonly operator: "equals" | "atLeast" | "atMost";
  readonly value: string | number;
}

/**
 * A rule, as a tree.
 *
 * The shape composition produces. Each combinator adds a node rather than
 * closing over a function, which is what keeps a composite rule as legible to a
 * translator as the leaves it was built from.
 */
export type OrderQuery =
  | { readonly kind: "criterion"; readonly criterion: OrderCriterion }
  | { readonly kind: "every"; readonly nodes: readonly OrderQuery[] }
  | { readonly kind: "some"; readonly nodes: readonly OrderQuery[] }
  | { readonly kind: "complement"; readonly node: OrderQuery };

/**
 * A named rule, and what satisfying it establishes.
 *
 * The type parameter is what a satisfied candidate is known to be, defaulting
 * to no refinement so that a rule which establishes nothing beyond itself needs
 * no annotation.
 */
export interface OrderSpecification<N extends Order = Order> {
  /** What this rule is, readable by anything that wants to push it down. */
  readonly query: OrderQuery;

  /**
   * Whether the candidate satisfies the rule — and, in the type, what
   * satisfying it establishes.
   *
   * A type predicate rather than a `boolean`. The difference is the pattern's
   * contribution here: `filter` over this yields a list whose element type
   * records that the rule held, so a function requiring a paid order accepts
   * the result and refuses an unfiltered list.
   *
   * Worth knowing before annotating a call site: writing `: boolean` on a
   * predicate passed to `filter` silently disables the inference that makes
   * this work, so the narrowing is lost to a change that looks like an
   * improvement.
   */
  isSatisfiedBy(candidate: Order): candidate is N;

  /**
   * Both rules. The refinements intersect, so the result narrows by everything
   * checked.
   */
  and<M extends Order>(other: OrderSpecification<M>): OrderSpecification<N & M>;

  /**
   * Either rule. The refinements union, which is the most that can honestly be
   * claimed.
   */
  or<M extends Order>(other: OrderSpecification<M>): OrderSpecification<N | M>;

  /**
   * The opposite rule, with the refinement given up.
   *
   * Not an oversight, and the reason is worth stating because the alternative
   * looks better and is wrong. `Exclude<Order, N>` appears to name the
   * complement; it is `Order` itself, since `Exclude` distributes over unions
   * and `Order` is not one. Declaring that as the result would compile —
   * TypeScript checks no predicate's logic — and would hand back the unrefined
   * type under a name claiming otherwise. Giving it up says what is true.
   */
  not(): OrderSpecification;
}

/**
 * Builds a specification from a predicate and its description.
 *
 * Internal, because every rule should arrive through a named leaf below. A
 * specification assembled inline at a call site is the unnamed condition this
 * pattern exists to replace.
 */
function specification<N extends Order>(
  predicate: (candidate: Order) => candidate is N,
  query: OrderQuery,
): OrderSpecification<N> {
  return {
    isSatisfiedBy: predicate,
    query,
    and<M extends Order>(
      other: OrderSpecification<M>,
    ): OrderSpecification<N & M> {
      return specification(
        (candidate): candidate is N & M =>
          predicate(candidate) && other.isSatisfiedBy(candidate),
        { kind: "every", nodes: [query, other.query] },
      );
    },
    or<M extends Order>(
      other: OrderSpecification<M>,
    ): OrderSpecification<N | M> {
      return specification(
        (candidate): candidate is N | M =>
          predicate(candidate) || other.isSatisfiedBy(candidate),
        { kind: "some", nodes: [query, other.query] },
      );
    },
    not(): OrderSpecification {
      return specification(
        (candidate): candidate is Order => !predicate(candidate),
        { kind: "complement", node: query },
      );
    },
  };
}

/**
 * The fields a magnitude comparison makes sense on.
 *
 * Derived from the subject rather than listed, so a field that changes type is
 * either still comparable or no longer offered, and never merely assumed.
 */
type NumericField = {
  [K in keyof Order]: Order[K] extends number ? K : never;
}[keyof Order];

/**
 * A rule that a field holds a particular value.
 *
 * The refinement is derived from the value rather than restated, which is what
 * makes the declarative form free: `whereEquals("status", "paid")` narrows
 * exactly as a hand-written guard would, and there is no second place for the
 * two to disagree.
 *
 * The signature also does the checking a hand-written rule would not. An
 * unknown field is refused, and so is a value the field cannot hold — a rule
 * that no candidate could ever satisfy is a mistake worth catching where it is
 * written rather than in whatever fails to happen later.
 */
export function whereEquals<K extends keyof Order, V extends Order[K]>(
  field: K,
  value: V,
): OrderSpecification<Order & Readonly<Record<K, V>>> {
  return specification(
    (candidate): candidate is Order & Readonly<Record<K, V>> =>
      candidate[field] === value,
    { kind: "criterion", criterion: { field, operator: "equals", value } },
  );
}

/**
 * Rules about magnitude.
 *
 * No refinement, because there is none to have: that a total is at least a
 * hundred is not something a type can record about it. Claiming one here would
 * be the same error `not` avoids, and the honest signature is the unrefined
 * one.
 */
export function whereAtLeast<K extends NumericField>(
  field: K,
  value: number,
): OrderSpecification {
  return specification(
    (candidate): candidate is Order => (candidate[field] as number) >= value,
    { kind: "criterion", criterion: { field, operator: "atLeast", value } },
  );
}

export function whereAtMost<K extends NumericField>(
  field: K,
  value: number,
): OrderSpecification {
  return specification(
    (candidate): candidate is Order => (candidate[field] as number) <= value,
    { kind: "criterion", criterion: { field, operator: "atMost", value } },
  );
}

/**
 * How each operator is spelled.
 */
const OPERATORS: Readonly<Record<OrderCriterion["operator"], string>> = {
  equals: "=",
  atLeast: ">=",
  atMost: "<=",
};

/**
 * The rule as something a datastore can answer.
 *
 * The point of translation: without it, a rule can only be applied to rows
 * already fetched, so the filter costs a full read however selective it is.
 *
 * Values become placeholders rather than text, so nothing a caller supplies is
 * ever spliced into the statement. Field names *are* spliced, which would be
 * the obvious hole — and is closed by the type rather than by escaping: `field`
 * is `keyof Order`, so the only strings that can reach it are property names of
 * a type declared in this file. A caller cannot pass an arbitrary one because a
 * caller cannot name one.
 *
 * The empty forms render as constants rather than as empty parentheses, which
 * keeps the output valid SQL for a tree the free combinators can build.
 */
export function toSql(rule: OrderSpecification): {
  readonly text: string;
  readonly parameters: readonly (string | number)[];
} {
  const parameters: (string | number)[] = [];
  const text = render(rule.query, parameters);

  return { text, parameters };
}

function render(node: OrderQuery, parameters: (string | number)[]): string {
  switch (node.kind) {
    case "criterion": {
      parameters.push(node.criterion.value);

      return `${node.criterion.field} ${OPERATORS[node.criterion.operator]} ?`;
    }
    case "every": {
      if (node.nodes.length === 0) return "1 = 1";

      return `(${node.nodes.map((each) => render(each, parameters)).join(" AND ")})`;
    }
    case "some": {
      if (node.nodes.length === 0) return "1 = 0";

      return `(${node.nodes.map((each) => render(each, parameters)).join(" OR ")})`;
    }
    case "complement": {
      return `NOT ${render(node.node, parameters)}`;
    }
  }
}

## order-specification-example.ts (example)

```ts
/**
 * @generated by patterns — regenerate rather than edit.
 * @pattern specification
 * @options e284827a0b48e403
 */

/**
 * Rules with names, composed, and applied.
 *
 * The refusals at the end are assertions rather than illustrations:
 * `@ts-expect-error` is satisfied by an error and violated by silence, so each
 * states that the line below it must not compile. They are emitted whether or
 * not tests were asked for, because a specification that has quietly stopped
 * refining behaves identically at run time to one that has not, and only the
 * compiler can tell them apart.
 */

import {
  toSql,
  whereAtLeast,
  whereAtMost,
  whereEquals,
} from "./order-specification.js";
import type { Order, OrderQuery } from "./order-specification.js";

/**
 * The rules, each with a name.
 *
 * This is the pattern. A condition written inline at the place it is needed
 * cannot be reused, cannot be composed, cannot be tested on its own, and cannot
 * be discussed — and the name is what a reader of the composite below is
 * actually reading.
 *
 * Each is bound to a name before being combined for a second reason, which is a
 * compiler detail rather than a matter of style: inferred inside a nested call
 * the literal widens to the whole property type with `strictNullChecks` off,
 * and the refinement is lost. The idiomatic form is also the one whose types
 * hold everywhere.
 */
export const paid = whereEquals("status", "paid");
export const cancelled = whereEquals("status", "cancelled");
export const substantial = whereAtLeast("total", 100);

/**
 * Composites, which are rules too.
 *
 * Nothing distinguishes a combined rule from a leaf — it has a name, it tests a
 * candidate, and it can be combined again. That closure is what makes the
 * pattern worth having over a bag of helper functions.
 */
export const collectable = paid.and(substantial);
export const ignorable = cancelled.or(substantial.not());

/**
 * What the refinement is for.
 *
 * The parameter requires a paid order, and no cast, check, or comment gets a
 * caller past it — only having filtered. That is the difference between a rule
 * that returns `boolean` and one that returns a type predicate: the first
 * leaves everyone downstream to be careful, the second makes carelessness fail
 * to compile.
 */
export function receipt(order: Order & { readonly status: "paid" }): string {
  return `${order.id}: ${String(order.total)} paid`;
}

export function receipts(orders: readonly Order[]): readonly string[] {
  // The filter is what changes the element type, so `receipt` is applicable
  // here and would not be on the unfiltered list.
  return orders.filter(paid.isSatisfiedBy).map(receipt);
}

/**
 * The same rule, asked of the datastore instead.
 *
 * One declaration produced both of these, which is the property worth the
 * constraint that leaves be declarative: there is no second expression of the
 * rule to drift from the first, so the rows this selects and the candidates the
 * predicate accepts cannot come apart.
 */
export function collectableRows(): {
  readonly text: string;
  readonly parameters: readonly (string | number)[];
} {
  return toSql(collectable);
}

export function describe(query: OrderQuery): string {
  return query.kind;
}

/**
 * The refusals, asserted.
 *
 * Each directive sits alone on its line with the reason above it, because a
 * directive governs only the line it begins on and a long comment gets
 * re-wrapped by the formatter.
 */

export function refusesAnUnrefinedOrder(order: Order): void {
  // The guarantee, stated as a compile error: nothing here establishes that
  // this one is paid, and `receipt` says so rather than trusting its caller.
  //
  // Written as a direct call on purpose. The shorter spelling — passing
  // `receipt` to `map` over an unfiltered list — asserts nothing reliably,
  // because `strictFunctionTypes` is part of `strict` and without it function
  // parameters are compared bivariantly, so a callback wanting the narrower
  // type is accepted where the wider one is expected. That version compiles
  // under a loose config, which makes the directive unused and the file stop
  // building on the wrong thing. Argument assignability at a direct call is
  // invariant everywhere, so this holds at every strictness.
  //
  // @ts-expect-error
  receipt(order);
}

export function refusesToNarrowThroughNegation(orders: readonly Order[]): void {
  const notPaid = paid.not();

  // `not` gives up the refinement, deliberately: the complement of a refinement
  // is not expressible, and the type that appears to name it — `Exclude` —
  // silently returns the unrefined type. So the chain stops narrowing here, and
  // that is the honest outcome rather than a gap.
  //
  // Asserted as an assignment rather than a call for the same reason as above:
  // array assignability is covariant in the element type and unaffected by how
  // function parameters are compared.
  //
  // @ts-expect-error
  const paidOnly: readonly (Order & { readonly status: "paid" })[] =
    orders.filter(notPaid.isSatisfiedBy);
  void paidOnly;
}

export function refusesAnUnknownField(): void {
  // A field the subject does not have. Caught where the rule is written rather
  // than wherever its absence eventually shows.
  //
  // @ts-expect-error
  whereEquals("nonesuch", 1);
}

export function refusesAnImpossibleValue(): void {
  // A value the field cannot hold. This is a rule no candidate could satisfy,
  // which is always a mistake and never a subtle one.
  //
  // @ts-expect-error
  whereEquals("status", "shipped");
}

export function refusesAMagnitudeOnText(): void {
  // `status` is not a number, so there is no ordering to compare against.
  // @ts-expect-error
  whereAtLeast("status", 1);
}
```

## order-specification.test-d.ts (test)

```ts
/**
 * @generated by patterns — regenerate rather than edit.
 * @pattern specification
 * @options e284827a0b48e403
 */

/**
 * What the compiler is asked to prove.
 *
 * Nothing here runs. The suffix keeps the file out of every runner while
 * leaving it in front of the compiler, which is the only thing that can check
 * these claims: a specification that has stopped refining filters exactly the
 * same candidates as one that has not, so no suite that executes could tell the
 * difference.
 *
 * No claim below concerns nullability. Bundles are verified at every
 * strictness, and with `strictNullChecks` off `undefined` is assignable to
 * everything, so such an assertion would mean one thing for one caller and the
 * opposite for another.
 */

import {
  toSql,
  whereAtLeast,
  whereAtMost,
  whereEquals,
} from "./order-specification.js";
import type { Order } from "./order-specification.js";

/**
 * Forces its argument to be `true`, and fails to compile when it is not.
 *
 * Each assertion below is written as a named alias rather than a bare one, so
 * that it reads as a stated claim about the code and cannot be mistaken for a
 * leftover.
 */
export type Expect<T extends true> = T;

/**
 * Whether two types are identical, rather than merely assignable in both
 * directions.
 *
 * The two-function form looks like a trick because it is one: it compares the
 * types in a position the compiler checks by identity instead of by
 * assignability. The obvious alternative — asking whether each extends the
 * other — answers a different question, and answers it wrongly in two common
 * cases. It reports `true` for `any` against anything at all, and it
 * distributes over unions, so a union compared against one of its own members
 * can come back true.
 */
export type Equal<X, Y> =
  (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends <T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2
    ? true
    : false;

/**
 * Whether `X` is assignable to `Y`.
 *
 * Both sides are wrapped in a tuple to stop the union distribution a bare
 * conditional performs. Undistributed is the question that was meant: whether
 * the whole of `X` is acceptable as a `Y`, rather than whether each member of
 * it is on its own.
 */
export type Extends<X, Y> = [X] extends [Y] ? true : false;

/**
 * Whether `X` is rejected where a `Y` is wanted.
 *
 * The type-level counterpart to `@ts-expect-error`, and preferable wherever the
 * claim is about a relationship rather than about a particular line: a
 * directive suppresses whichever error occurs, so it can be satisfied by an
 * unrelated mistake on the same line, where this cannot.
 */
export type NotAssignable<X, Y> = [X] extends [Y] ? false : true;

/**
 * The rules under test, declared as the example declares them.
 *
 * Repeated here rather than imported so that this file states its own subject:
 * a compile-time claim reads as an argument, and an argument whose premises are
 * elsewhere is harder to check.
 */
const paid = whereEquals("status", "paid");
const cancelled = whereEquals("status", "cancelled");
const substantial = whereAtLeast("total", 100);

declare const orders: readonly Order[];

/**
 * Filtering by a rule changes the element type.
 *
 * The pattern's contribution in one assertion. Everything else here is about
 * what survives.
 */
const filtered = orders.filter(paid.isSatisfiedBy);
export type FilteringRefines = Expect<
  Extends<(typeof filtered)[number], { readonly status: "paid" }>
>;
export type UnfilteredDoesNot = Expect<
  NotAssignable<Order, { readonly status: "paid" }>
>;

/**
 * Composition keeps the refinement, however deep.
 *
 * Both of these, because a combinator that returned the unrefined type would
 * still compile everywhere and would quietly cost every call site downstream
 * its guarantee. The three-deep case is separate because preserving one level
 * and losing the next is a plausible way to be wrong.
 */
const bothFiltered = orders.filter(paid.and(substantial).isSatisfiedBy);
export type CompositionRefines = Expect<
  Extends<(typeof bothFiltered)[number], { readonly status: "paid" }>
>;

const deeplyFiltered = orders.filter(
  paid.and(substantial).and(substantial).isSatisfiedBy,
);
export type DeepCompositionRefines = Expect<
  Extends<(typeof deeplyFiltered)[number], { readonly status: "paid" }>
>;

/**
 * Negation gives the refinement up, exactly.
 *
 * `Equal` rather than `NotAssignable`, because the claim is not merely that the
 * refinement is weaker — it is that the result is the plain subject. That is
 * what rules out the tempting wrong version, where `Exclude` produces something
 * that reads as a complement and is the subject in disguise.
 */
const negated = orders.filter(paid.not().isSatisfiedBy);
export type NegationErasesRefinement = Expect<
  Equal<(typeof negated)[number], Order>
>;

/**
 * A union is the most an alternative can claim.
 *
 * Neither side alone holds, so nothing narrower than the union would be true —
 * and the union is worth having, since a discriminated subject stays narrowable
 * afterwards.
 */
const either = orders.filter(paid.or(cancelled).isSatisfiedBy);
export type AlternativeUnions = Expect<
  Extends<(typeof either)[number], { readonly status: "paid" | "cancelled" }>
>;
```

## order-specification.test.ts (test)

```ts
/**
 * @generated by patterns — regenerate rather than edit.
 * @pattern specification
 * @options e284827a0b48e403
 */

/**
 * What is left for a suite that runs.
 *
 * Not the refinements, which are settled before this file executes and asserted
 * in `order-specification.test-d.ts`. What remains is which candidates each
 * rule actually accepts, and whether composition means what it says — a rule
 * that refined correctly and matched the wrong candidates would satisfy every
 * claim in that file.
 */

import { describe, expect, it } from "vitest";

import {
  toSql,
  whereAtLeast,
  whereAtMost,
  whereEquals,
} from "./order-specification.js";
import type { Order } from "./order-specification.js";

const paid = whereEquals("status", "paid");
const cancelled = whereEquals("status", "cancelled");
const substantial = whereAtLeast("total", 100);

// Three candidates, chosen so that no two rules select the same subset —
// otherwise a composite could agree with its parts by accident and the
// composition assertions would prove nothing.
const draft: Order = { id: "A-1", total: 500, status: "draft" };
const smallPaid: Order = { id: "A-2", total: 10, status: "paid" };
const largePaid: Order = { id: "A-3", total: 500, status: "paid" };
const orders: readonly Order[] = [draft, smallPaid, largePaid];

describe("a named rule", () => {
  it("selects what it describes and nothing else", () => {
    expect(orders.filter(paid.isSatisfiedBy)).toEqual([smallPaid, largePaid]);
    expect(orders.filter(substantial.isSatisfiedBy)).toEqual([
      draft,
      largePaid,
    ]);
  });

  it("answers about a single candidate", () => {
    expect(paid.isSatisfiedBy(largePaid)).toBe(true);
    expect(paid.isSatisfiedBy(draft)).toBe(false);
  });

  it("includes a candidate sitting exactly on the threshold", () => {
    // The one input that distinguishes an inclusive comparison from an
    // exclusive one. Without it a rule spelled `>` where `>=` was meant selects
    // the same candidates as the correct version on every other input, so the
    // fixture above cannot see the difference and this case exists to.
    const atThreshold: Order = { id: "A-4", total: 100, status: "paid" };

    expect(substantial.isSatisfiedBy(atThreshold)).toBe(true);
  });
});

describe("composition", () => {
  it("requires both rules, not either", () => {
    // `largePaid` alone satisfies both. Asserting the whole selection rather
    // than its length is what distinguishes an intersection from a union here,
    // since the union has two members.
    const both = paid.and(substantial);

    expect(orders.filter(both.isSatisfiedBy)).toEqual([largePaid]);
  });

  it("accepts either rule", () => {
    const either = paid.or(cancelled);

    expect(orders.filter(either.isSatisfiedBy)).toEqual([smallPaid, largePaid]);
  });

  it("inverts a rule", () => {
    expect(orders.filter(paid.not().isSatisfiedBy)).toEqual([draft]);
  });

  it("composes a composite", () => {
    const nested = paid.and(substantial).or(cancelled);

    expect(orders.filter(nested.isSatisfiedBy)).toEqual([largePaid]);
  });
});

describe("translation", () => {
  it("bounds a magnitude from either side, inclusively", () => {
    // `whereAtMost` is otherwise unreached by this suite, and both boundaries
    // are inclusive, so both are asserted at the value where inclusivity is the
    // only thing being tested.
    const modest = whereAtMost("total", 100);
    const atThreshold: Order = { id: "A-4", total: 100, status: "paid" };

    expect(modest.isSatisfiedBy(atThreshold)).toBe(true);
    expect(modest.isSatisfiedBy(largePaid)).toBe(false);
    expect(toSql(modest).text).toBe("total <= ?");
  });

  it("renders a leaf with the value as a parameter", () => {
    const { text, parameters } = toSql(paid);

    // The value is a placeholder and the field is not, which is the one splice
    // in the renderer and is safe because `keyof` closes the set of strings
    // that can reach it.
    expect(text).toBe("status = ?");
    expect(parameters).toEqual(["paid"]);
  });

  it("renders a composite, keeping the parameters in the order they appear", () => {
    const { text, parameters } = toSql(paid.and(substantial));

    expect(text).toBe("(status = ? AND total >= ?)");
    expect(parameters).toEqual(["paid", 100]);
  });

  it("renders an alternative and a negation", () => {
    expect(toSql(paid.or(cancelled)).text).toBe("(status = ? OR status = ?)");
    expect(toSql(paid.not()).text).toBe("NOT status = ?");
  });

  it("keeps the predicate and the query answering the same question", () => {
    // Not provable by a test — one declaration produces both, so there is no
    // second expression to disagree — but the parameters a rule renders should
    // be the values its predicate compares against, and a leaf that translated
    // one field while testing another would show up here.
    const { text, parameters } = toSql(substantial);

    expect(text).toBe("total >= ?");
    expect(parameters).toEqual([100]);
    expect(substantial.isSatisfiedBy(largePaid)).toBe(true);
    expect(substantial.isSatisfiedBy(smallPaid)).toBe(false);
  });
});
```
